Open Policy Analysis for:

California Proposition 40, Reconciliation of the Two Analyses

Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act, would tax Californians worth $1 billion or more once, at 5% of their net worth, paid over five years. The BSZ analysis (Boll, Saez and Zucman, NBER, August 2026) finds that it raises money for the state. The JR analysis (Jaros and Rauh, NBER, September 2026) finds that it leaves the state $38.9B poorer, because billionaires who leave stop paying California income tax for ever. This page puts both on one definition and shows which assumptions make the difference. It follows the Open Policy Analysis (OPA) framework.

BSZ main estimate1 $106.8B Net total: the wealth tax plus the income tax it changes, over 5 years, in today's dollars
JR main estimate1 −$38.9B Net present value: the wealth tax minus the income tax lost for ever, in today's dollars, averaged over the authors' model runs (Jaros and Rauh, September 2026)

Today's dollars (present value): what money received or lost in future years is worth now.

What separates the two numbers

$106.8BBSZ estimate −$28.2BBillionaires already departed (D)path at $72.6B −$41.4BChance the tax survives litigation (q)path at $40.1B −$58.9BHow long the income tax loss lasts (H)path at −$26.8B −$10.6BThe other five steps together ≈−$32.3BJR estimate at one 3% rate

The JR analysis's own headline is −$38.9B: the authors draw the discount rate at random between 1.5% and 4.5% and average, which is worth about $6.7B more than one 3% rate.

Move the BSZ panel's dials top to bottom, each to its far end. The three terms with a symbol are the steps for D, q and H of that walk, and the fourth is the other five steps added up (W, a, f, C and three minor inputs). Under each of the three is the value the path reaches after that step. The explorer does it for you. The report gives all eight steps.

A common output definition #

one definition both numbers can be put on, and the conventions behind it

The two headlines answer different questions: the BSZ analysis reports what the tax collects, the JR analysis a net present value that subtracts income tax lost for ever. Both are put on two outputs. The explorer shows (b); (a) is in the report.

(b) net fiscal effect = (a) + extra income tax from assets sold to pay - present value of income tax lost to departures, over a horizon of H years (a) gross revenue = one-time wealth tax collected

The horizon H is itself disputed: about the 5 payment years for the BSZ analysis, for ever for the JR analysis. So it is a dial in the explorer and a step of the bridge. Present values use one discount rate, 3% a year, the rate the BSZ overview uses. The BSZ analysis takes no position on the rate. The JR analysis draws it at random; that is a method of the JR analysis, not a disputed input, and the note under the equation above gives what it is worth.

Conventions. Nominal billions of dollars. The wealth tax is counted at face value when assessed and not discounted over the five installments, as both analyses do. The BSZ analysis values the base on 1 July 2026; the JR analysis grows its 2025 Forbes base by 7% to 31 December 2026. The JR code labels its rate draw r − g and its text r (the JR analysis's mismatch 3).

What this OPA does not estimate. Both analyses, and so this OPA, take the measure as written (docs/initiative/). Neither models the day-to-day movement of the Forbes base. Nothing is added to either analysis here.

The two analyses on the common output #

both main estimates on that definition, and what each paper prints
BSZ analysis: a revenue estimate

Boll, Saez, Zucman, NBER WP 35218 (Aug 2026) →

Static estimation on the Forbes list with a 10% avoidance allowance.

Main estimate, net total: $106.8B Table 5 row 1, wealth tax: $103.8B (the paper prints $104B)
JR analysis: a net present value estimate

Jaros and Rauh, NBER c15504 (Sep 2026) →

Person-by-person base, observed departures, a litigation weight, lost income tax for ever.

Main estimate, mean NPV: −$38.9B
Analysis(b) net fiscal effect(a) gross revenueWhat the authors print
BSZ analysis: Boll, Saez and Zucman, NBER WP 35218, Table 5 row 1 (Aug 2026)$106.8B$103.8B$104B revenue (PDF p.39); no net figure
JR analysis: Jaros and Rauh, NBER c15504 (Sep 2026), at one 3% rate−$32.25B$36.0Bmean NPV −$38.9B, with a random rate: $6.73B below the one-rate value (the JR rate gap); revenue 'approximately $30B' (p.1)

The BSZ paper prints no (b). It is Table 5 row 1's own columns combined here: $103.8B of revenue, plus $3.68B from asset sales, minus $0.70B, five years of its $0.15B yearly income tax loss. For the JR analysis, (a) is the exact mean revenue of the authors' Monte Carlo, drawn between zero and $72B. Its (b) is the JR inputs at one 3% rate. The authors' mean NPV is $6.7B lower, because they draw the rate at random (the note under the equation).

Row 3: % = 1 − 72 / 100.906, the authors' ceiling after seven departures over the grown base. Their person-level file gives 72.05 (mismatch 4); the script's 72 is used so the comparison returns their expected revenue exactly.

"A vs B" reads the BSZ value's kind against the JR value's; "guesswork on data" is a judgement applied to observed facts.

Other estimates of the yearly income tax loss, for scale #

the Legislative Analyst, the California Tax Foundation and both analyses' own figures on one scale

The LAO (the Legislative Analyst's Office, the state's nonpartisan fiscal adviser) gives no point estimate: responses "probably would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year" (p.2). Walczak (California Tax Foundation, 22 April 2026) puts the loss at $3.53-4.49B a year, spillovers included (p.1); he is credited as an alternative view, not merged into either analysis. This OPA and the Hoopes comparison #

the one published comparison, and what this OPA adds

Jeffrey Hoopes (SSRN 6428578, 2026) is the one published comparison of the two estimates. It compares earlier versions: the February 2026 GGSS expert report (Galle, Gamage, Saez and Shanske), on which the BSZ analysis builds, and the March 2026 JR analysis. Its Figure 2 prints no values and comes with no code or data, so its steps cannot be recomputed. This OPA uses the latest versions, publishes the code, and bridges the two estimates step by step. The report sets his bars beside this bridge, difference by difference.

1 Each analysis's own main estimate. The BSZ number is this OPA's net total over 5 years at 3%: the $103.8B wealth tax (Table 5 row 1), plus income tax from asset sales, minus income tax lost to leavers. BSZ's own headline is the wealth tax alone. The JR number is the authors' mean net present value in perpetuity. The report gives the details.
